p: High Wycombe was built on furniture. For generations the town was famous for making chairs, especially the classic Windsor chair, using beech from the Chiltern woods all around it. That heritage is why Wycombe Wanderers are nicknamed the Chairboys, and their ground, Adams Park, isn't far from Cressex Business Park, so expect busier roads on home match days.

If you'd like to learn more, Wycombe Museum on Priory Avenue tells the story of the chair-making trade and the town, set in an old house with gardens. For fresh air closer to the centre, The Rye is a long stretch of parkland with water, play areas and room for a kickabout.

Keep your eyes on the sky while you're driving around. Red kites were reintroduced to the Chilterns decades ago and are now a common sight circling over the town and the hills, with their forked tails and lazy gliding. Kids love counting them, and it's a nice way to fill a car journey.

Just west of town, the village of West Wycombe is home to the Hellfire Caves, a set of man-made tunnels with a colourful and slightly spooky history that older kids find fascinating. Over in Beaconsfield, Bekonscot Model Village is a charming little world in miniature, ideal for younger children.
With the M40 so close, it's easy to arrive, bounce, explore and be home in time for tea.
A good rhythm for the day is bounce in the morning, picnic on The Rye at lunchtime, then a gentle drive out into the Chilterns villages for the afternoon, with kite-spotting all the way.
